title: Judges, Ruth, Esther, Song: some books lack intrinsic notes strong enough for faith's certainty
source_text: XXXIII. Praesertim vero, si singulos Scripturae sacrae libros consideremus, fatendum est multos esse qui in se non habeant eas divinitatis notas, quibus necessario et evidenter probetur authoritas eorum divina, et quibus tanta possit fundari certitudo, quantam fides requirit. Quales sunt, exempli gratia, liber Judicum, liber Ruth, liber Esther, Canticum Canticorum, quos divinitus inspiratos esse, vix probari potest aliis argumentis, quam generalibus illis, quae petuntur a testimonio et consensu Ecclesiae Judaicae et Christianae. Et tamen libri illi sunt pars verbi divini, et regulae illius fidei certissimae, ad quam omnia, quae religionem spectant, exigenda sunt et examinanda; adeoque pertinent ad fidei objectum in tota sua amplitudine sumptum: et assensus quem illis, sicuti par est, praebemus, non refertur ad aliam virtutem, quam ad fidem. Ac proinde, cum partes quaedam verbi Dei fide suscipiendae non habeant ea divinitatis argumenta, quae per se fundare possint assensum tam certum quam fides exigit, proculdubio argumenta, quibus verbum Dei divinum se probat et a Deo manasse, non sunt praecipuum fidei fundamentum, et ultimum illud in quod fides nostra resolvi debet. Neque ad rem pertinet quod librorum ejusmodi fides ad singulorum salutem necessaria non est. Hic enim non est quaestio, quid ad singulorum salutem necessarium sit, vel non. Sed consideramus in genere naturam, et fundamentum fidei ad cujus objectum pertinent multa, quae non sunt cognitu singulis ad salutem necessaria.
pass_a_gloss: Especially indeed, if we consider the individual books of sacred Scripture, it must be confessed that there are many which do not have in themselves those notes of divinity by which their divine authority is necessarily and evidently proved, and by which so great a certainty can be founded as faith requires. Such are, for example, the book of Judges, the book of Ruth, the book of Esther, the Song of Songs, which can scarcely be proved to be divinely inspired by other arguments than those general ones drawn from the testimony and consent of the Jewish and Christian Church. And yet those books are part of the divine Word, and of that most certain rule of faith to which everything that concerns religion must be brought and examined; and so they belong to the object of faith taken in its whole amplitude; and the assent we duly give them is referred to no other virtue than to faith. And therefore, since certain parts of God's Word that must be received by faith do not have those arguments of divinity which of themselves can found an assent as certain as faith demands, without doubt the arguments by which God's Word proves itself divine and as having come from God are not the principal foundation of faith, and that last thing into which our faith ought to be resolved. Nor does it matter that faith in books of that sort is not necessary for the salvation of individuals. For here the question is not what is necessary for each person's salvation, or not. But we are considering in general the nature and foundation of faith, to whose object many things belong that are not necessary for individuals to know for salvation.
pass_b_english: Especially when we take the sacred books one by one, we must admit that many do not carry in themselves those notes of divinity that would necessarily and evidently prove their divine authority, or found the certainty faith requires. Judges, Ruth, Esther, and the Song of Songs are examples. That they are divinely inspired can scarcely be proved by anything but the general arguments drawn from the testimony and consent of the Jewish and Christian Church.

Yet those books are part of the divine Word and of that most certain rule of faith by which everything that touches religion must be tried and examined. They belong to the object of faith in its full breadth, and the assent we rightly give them is referred to no other virtue than faith. So when some parts of God's Word that faith must receive lack intrinsic arguments of divinity strong enough by themselves to found the assent faith demands, the arguments by which God's Word proves itself divine and from God are plainly not faith's principal foundation, or the last thing into which our faith should resolve.

It is no answer that faith in such books is not necessary for each person's salvation. The question here is not what each person must know to be saved. We are considering the nature and foundation of faith in general — and many things belong to faith's object that individuals need not know for salvation.
